title: Buccal Fat Removal , Part 1
transcript: Hi everyone, it's Dr. Sharma here, and today we're going to be talking all about buccal fat removal. Buccal fat removal is becoming a very popular surgery for people who are looking to take out all that extra chubbiness in their cheeks and to slim and taper the lower 2/3 of their face. So, what is buccal fat? Who's a good candidate for surgery, and how do we take it out? The buccal fat pad is one of the deep fat pads of the face, meaning it lies deep to your SMAS fascia and the muscles that control facial movement. Now, the fat pad itself is actually quite large with its anterior lobe sitting in the buccal space of your cheek, and that's a part of your dressing surgery, extending up underneath your bony zygomatic arch, which defines the height of your cheekbone, and going all the way up into your temporal fossa, lying below your temporalis muscle. Now, as a deep fat pad, buccal fat does not respond to weight gain or weight loss like superficial fat on the rest of your body. Instead, it slowly grows in size between the ages of 10 and 20, and then after your teenage years, it progressively starts to atrophy or shrink. title: Mohs surgery isn’t just about clearing the visible tumor — it’s about knowing when to look deeper. 🩺
transcript: So, I recently had a really interesting Mohs case. So, Mohs is micrographic surgery to help clear tumors of the skin. Particularly, usually it's basal cell or squamous cell skin cancers. So, this particular patient had a squamous cell skin cancer. And just because you're necessarily clear on the Mohs slides, which is what normally would happen, sometimes that's not always the case. And I think this is where experience comes into play. So, I've been doing Mohs for a few years. And what I found is that if I see a really aggressive tumor on the first stage of Mohs, I keep going until it's clear. But then what I do is package everything up and send it off to my um pathologist. And then they will special stain it and go through the remainder of the block. I know this gets a little bit technical, but what they do is look at the remainder of the center tissue to see if potentially there's any perineural involvement. Perineural involvement means that the skin cancer has actually started to wrap around nerves. And it what happens is that it can actually skip down the nerve. So, you may have a clear margin with Mohs, but the skin cancer may have skipped down. Now, this is very rare. So, this is really more with just aggressive tumors. And you can see that morphology on the slides when you're looking at it. And you kind of have maybe a guess or a hunch that this is a really an aggressive tumor. I should have my pathologist actually immunostain specifically to look at the nerves. So, one thing to think about.

caption:
😳🔴 A boil isn't just a bump...

It's a pocket of pus forming beneath your skin.

Boils develop when bacteria infect a **hair follicle** or nearby oil gland. Your immune system responds by sending white blood cells to fight the infection, leading to a buildup of pus.

⚠️ As pressure increases, the area becomes red, swollen, warm, and painful.

💡 Most boils heal with proper treatment, but large, recurrent, or spreading boils should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.

#Boils #SkinInfection #HumanBody #MedicalEducation #HealthAwareness #Dermatology

transcript: A boil doesn't suddenly appear. It starts when bacteria get trapped deep inside a hair follicle. Your immune system immediately attacks the bacteria. White blood cells flood the area. But as they die along with bacteria and damaged tissue, a thick pocket of pus begins to form beneath the skin. As more pus builds up, stretches the skin, causing pain and swelling. Eventually, the boil drains, releasing the trapped pus and allowing the infection to begin healing.

Fraxel laser treatments are a popular option for improving skin texture and reducing wrinkles, acne scars, and other skin irregularities. The progress of Fraxel laser treatment varies from person to person based on factors like skin type, the condition being treated, and the intensity of the treatment.



Here's a general timeline of what you might expect during and after Fraxel laser treatment:


During the treatment: The laser is passed over the skin, delivering tiny, controlled beams of light that penetrate the skin's surface, stimulating collagen production and triggering the body's natural healing process.


Immediate effects: After the treatment, you might experience redness and swelling, similar to a mild sunburn. This usually subsides within a few hours to a few days, depending on the intensity of the treatment.


Days 1-7: The skin will start to flake and peel as the damaged outer layer sheds, revealing fresher, smoother skin underneath. It's crucial to keep the skin moisturized and protected from the sun during this time.


Weeks 2-4: Collagen production is gradually stimulated, leading to continued improvement in skin texture and tone. You may notice a reduction in fine lines, wrinkles, and other imperfections during this period.


Months 2-6: The full results of the treatment typically become apparent within 2 to 6 months as collagen continues to remodel and the skin continues to improve in texture and appearance.

caption:
What say you? 🫵 Melanoma or not? 

At first glance, it appears dark blue to almost black, irregular, and nodular. Those are features that can overlap with melanoma, including some nodular melanomas.

But dermatology is about recognizing patterns, not just colors.

🔍 Dermoscopy revealed multiple blue to violaceous lacunae separated by pale septa, a classic vascular pattern consistent with a vascular malformation.

The color itself is fascinating. Although many people think veins are blue, the blood inside them is actually dark red, even when deoxygenated. The bluish appearance results from the way light interacts with the skin. Because this lesion lies deeper in the dermis, shorter blue wavelengths are preferentially scattered back to our eyes, a phenomenon known as the Tyndall effect.

In many ways, this is similar to a varicose vein, just in an unusual location.

By combining the clinical history with dermoscopy, this lesion could be recognized as benign and safely monitored without the need for a biopsy. 💙

#melanomaawareness #melanoma

•••

Fait intéressant, le sang veineux n’est pas bleu, mais rouge foncé. La teinte bleutée provient de la profondeur de la lésion et de la façon dont la lumière interagit avec la peau (effet Tyndall).

En quelque sorte, il s’agit d’une « varice » située à un endroit inhabituel.

on_screen_hook: Skin cancer 101 part 4. Not all skin cancer looks like an
transcript: Skin cancer 101 part 4. Not all skin cancer looks like an abnormal mole. Some skin cancers appear to be completely normal. Basal cell carcinoma can often appear as a shiny, pearly pink bump, and a lot of times they can actually look like normal pimples. But the thing that usually distinguishes A bcc from a pimple is that a basal cell carcinoma will hang around for months without ever fully healing. Another possible sign of skin cancer is a dry patch that won't go away no matter how much you moisturize. Or it can be a tiny delicate sore that bleeds just by washing your face. And melanoma isn't always brown or black. Some melanomas have very little pigment and can appear pink or skin coloured. We call these amelanotic melanomas, meaning they don't have the classic pigmented appearance. So rather than going based off of a few photos on what skin cancer should look like, focus on whether a spot is changing, growing, bleeding, crusting over, or just not healing. Tomorrow we'll talk all things basal cell carcinoma, so make sure to hit that follow button.

Curious about what it’s like to undergo Mohs surgery for Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)? Join Board Certified Mohs Surgeon & Dermatologisst, Dr. Brian Feinstein, as he performs this precise and highly effective procedure for skin cancer treatment.

Here’s the patient’s journey:
👨‍⚕️ After noticing suspicious spots, a biopsy revealed SCC—a common but potentially serious skin cancer.

💡 What is SCC?
SCC results from accelerated squamous cell growth and is curable when detected early.
Over 1.8 million cases are diagnosed annually in the U.S., with incidence rates increasing dramatically over the past 30 years.

Why Mohs Surgery?
Mohs surgery is the gold standard for treating skin cancer, removing cancerous layers one by one while sparing healthy tissue. Each layer is examined in real time to ensure all cancer cells are removed, offering the highest cure rates.

💥 Why Choose Dr. Feinstein?
With over 10,000 Mohs cases performed, Dr. Feinstein delivers unmatched precision and expertise, ensuring optimal results for every patient.

📅 If you have concerns about suspicious spots or have been diagnosed with SCC, schedule a consultation today. Early detection saves lives.

caption:
✨ AZELAIC ACID + TRETINOIN: A POWERFUL SKINCARE COMBINATION

Azelaic Acid (Aziderm 10% Cream) + Tretinoin (Tretin 0.05% Cream) can be a useful combination for acne, clogged pores, uneven skin tone, post-acne marks, fine lines and skin texture—but application and tolerance matter.

☀️ MORNING — Azelaic Acid
• Start Aziderm 10% only 1–2 mornings per week.
• If your skin tolerates it well, gradually increase to alternate mornings.
• Follow with a moisturizer.
• Finish with a broad-spectrum SPF 30–50 sunscreen.

🌙 NIGHT — Tretinoin
• Use only a pea-sized amount for the entire face. More product does NOT mean faster results.
• Start around 2 nights per week and gradually increase the frequency depending on your skin’s tolerance.
• Follow with a moisturizer to help manage dryness and irritation.
• Avoid applying tretinoin on/too close to the eyelids, eyes, lips and corners of the nose.

🔬 Why Tretinoin?
Tretinoin increases epidermal cell turnover and supports collagen remodeling. With consistent use, it can help improve:
• Acne & clogged pores
• Fine lines
• Uneven texture
• Appearance of photoaged skin

⚠️ The catch: Tretinoin can initially cause dryness, peeling, redness, burning and irritation, especially when introduced too aggressively.

🌿 Where does Azelaic Acid help?
Azelaic acid has anti-inflammatory and comedolytic properties and can help with:
• Acne
• Redness & inflammation
• Post-acne pigmentation
• Uneven skin tone

⚠️ Important: Azelaic acid can also sting or irritate sensitive skin, and Tretinoin 0.05% may be too strong for some beginners. Tretinoin should also be avoided during pregnancy. Ideally, start it under the guidance of your dermatologist.

📌 Save this post before starting your routine—and remember: consistency beats using stronger products too quickly.

Curious about laser treatments but unsure which one is right for you? Lets break down two of the most popular fractional laser technologies in this video: Clear + Brilliant and Fraxel Dual.

🔬 Both lasers use fractional technology, meaning they treat a portion of the skin at a time to stimulate collagen, improve texture, and promote cell turnover—while leaving surrounding skin intact for faster healing. But
they differ in depth, intensity, and purpose:

✨ Clear + Brilliant:
• A gentle, non-ablative laser
• Great for early prevention and maintenance
• Treats enlarged pores, mild pigment, uneven tone, and dullness
• Minimal downtime—think of it as a “laser facial”
• Ideal for patients in their 20s–30s or those looking for a skin refresh

🔥 Fraxel Dual:
• Targets deeper layers of skin
• Treats more advanced concerns like fine lines, wrinkles, sun damage, acne scars, and melasma
• Can require 3–7 days of recovery depending on treatment intensity
• Recommended for patients looking for corrective results and significant skin renewal

✅ Both lasers are safe for most skin types, and treatment plans can be customized based on your skin tone, goals, and lifestyle.

caption:
Here it goes!  

1. Stop pulling your hair back so tightly. Constant tension can cause traction alopecia, and over time that hair loss can become permanent.

2. Retinoids are one of the most effective ways to boost skin collagen. Retinol is my pick for starters, and adapalene is my pick for acne-prone skin.

3. Cystic acne is really hard to treat with over-the-counter products. Your time and money are better spent seeing a dermatologist early.

4. Skip the Russian manicures. Your cuticles protect your nails from infection and damage, so leave them alone.

5. Start yearly skin checks in your 20s. If you have a personal or family history of skin cancer, you may need them more often.

6. Go easy on eyebrow gels. Daily stiff gels and aggressive brushing can lead to breakage and thinning over time.

7. Use your hair dryer on low heat, at least 6 inches from your scalp.

8. Diet isn’t the only thing behind your acne. Stress, hormones and genetics play a big role too.

9. Exfoliate, but gently. Reach for AHAs if your skin is dry, BHAs if it’s oily, and skip the harsh scrubs.

10. Toss the magnifying mirror. No one is looking at your pores that closely, and you shouldn’t either.

caption:
A cirurgia de Mohs é uma técnica moderna usada para remover cânceres de pele com o máximo de precisão.

O procedimento funciona assim: o médico retira camadas bem finas da pele afetada e cada uma delas é analisada no microscópio, em tempo real. Se ainda houver células cancerosas, outra camada é removida e esse processo continua até que toda a área doente seja eliminada.

A grande vantagem é que apenas o tecido comprometido é retirado, preservando o máximo possível da pele saudável. Por isso, é muito indicada em áreas delicadas, como rosto, nariz e orelhas, ou em casos de cânceres com alto risco de recidiva.

📌 Com taxas de cura que chegam a 99% em alguns tipos de câncer de pele, a cirurgia de Mohs é considerada o padrão-ouro nesse tratamento.

👉 O diagnóstico precoce e a escolha da técnica correta fazem toda a diferença.

caption:
My top tips to repair your skin barrier👇

1. Completely stop using actives eg retinoids, exfoliants, vitamin c until your barrier is healed - even if you are using a retinoid for acne you should stop until your barrier is healed because a damaged barrier can cause breakouts and you need a healthy barrier first to effectively treat acne

2. Stick to a simple routine including a gentle cleanser - don’t use any harsh cleansers, scrubs or peels these can further damage your barrier

3. Use a barrier repair cream until your skin is no longer tight, flaky, dry, peeling or stinging (see my post from 22nd Nov for best barrier creams and 25th Nov for best for acne)

4. If barrier creams break you out use lighter barrier repair products like toners and serums instead

5. Wait till your barrier is healed (this can take 2-6 weeks) before introducing exfoliants and retinoids again and when you do be super cautious (start with only x1 product 2x per week and increase as tolerated - it’s also best to start with a gentle active like PHA or a low % retinal). A big cause of barrier damage is using actives that are too strong for your skin, using them daily or even using multiple actives at once when you don’t have the tolerance (and maybe never will) so you need to start low and slow to avoid damage and see what you tolerate

Let me know if you have any questions in the comments ❤️

transcript: Things I don't care about as a dermatologist. I don't care if you splash your face with cold water, warm water, or filtered water. Your skin doesn't care either. Just wash with a gentle cleanser that works for you. I don't care if your skincare has activated charcoal or fairy dust. Detoxing your skin isn't real. Your liver and kidneys have that part covered. I don't care if your serum comes in a glass dropper or plastic pump unless it's vitamin C. For everything else, focus on the ingredients, not the packaging. I don't care if your sunscreen leaves a white cast for 30 seconds. Protection is non negotiable. Blend it and go on with your day. I don't care if you've been told that coconut oil is a natural miracle for your face. It clogs pores and wrecks your barrier. So keep it in the kitchen. I don't care if your cleanser says for all skin types or pH balanced. What matters is how your skin feels after. If it feels tight, it's not good for your skin. I don't care if your skincare products are made with ancient remedies or super foods. Trendy ingredients don't mean better skin. Stick with proven ingredients. I don't care if someone swears that beef tallow will heal your skin. It's outdated, heavy, and pore clogging. Modern moisturizers are better for your skin barrier and better for your breakouts. I don't care if your products are labeled for men or for women. Skin Is skin and these labels are just marketing. And the pink tax often times means you're paying more for the same formula and prettier packaging. Use what works for your skin type, not your gender. I don't care if your skincare says chemical free. Everything is made of chemicals, including water. What matters is that the ingredients are safe and effective, not the marketing buzz words. At the end of the day, I don't care about the trends, the marketing, or the fancy claims. What I care about is healthy, happy skin, and that comes from science, not hype. Retinol, a derivative of vitamin A, is a potent skincare ingredient known for its ability to promote skin renewal and combat acne. When first introducing retinol into your skincare routine, it’s common to experience a ‘purge’ phase, where the skin may temporarily break out before improving. 

During this period of time, retinol accelerates cell turnover, shedding dead skin cells. This process may lead to an increase in breakouts  as the underlying impurities come to the surface, revealing a path to clearer skin! 

As the purge subsides, the real benefits of retinol unfolds. By regulating sebum (oil) production and preventing clogged pores, it reduces the breakouts and blackheads. 

As you embrace retinol in your skincare routine, remember to start with a low concentration and gradually increase usage to allow your skin to acclimate.

caption:
Toda mancha ou pinta na pele merece atenção?

A pele pode apresentar diversas lesões, desde alterações benignas até condições que exigem investigação urgente e tratamento específico.

Entre as lesões que podem surgir, estão:

⚜️ Angiomas rubis: pequenas lesões avermelhadas, geralmente benignas, formadas por vasos sanguíneos.

⚜️ Queratoses actínicas: lesões causadas pela exposição solar acumulada, consideradas pré-cancerosas e que precisam de acompanhamento. São mais comuns no rosto e membros superiores.

⚜️ Carcinoma basocelular: o tipo de câncer de pele mais comum, costuma apresentar crescimento lento, mas requer diagnóstico e tratamento. 

⚜️ Nevo melanocítico comum: as conhecidas pintas, geralmente benignas, que devem ser observadas quanto a mudanças de cor, formato ou tamanho.

⚜️ Herpes-zóster: infecção causada pela reativação do vírus da catapora, que pode provocar bolhas, dor e ardência.

⚜️ Queratose seborreica: lesão benigna que pode apresentar aspecto elevado e cor marrom.

⚜️ Melanoma: tipo de câncer de pele que pode surgir em uma pinta preexistente ou como uma nova lesão, exigindo diagnóstico precoce e pronta intervenção.

⚜️ Miliuns: pequenos cistos superficiais de queratina, geralmente esbranquiçados e benignos, comuns perto dos olhos.

⚠️É importante lembrar que nem toda lesão de pele é perigosa, mas alterações persistentes ou suspeitas precisam ser avaliadas. A aparência, isoladamente, nem sempre é suficiente para determinar o diagnóstico.
Se você percebeu alguma pinta ou lesão diferente, que está crescendo, mudando de aspecto, sangrando ou não cicatriza, procure um dermatologista para uma avaliação adequada.

caption:
Milia also referred to as “milk spots” are small, pearly white cysts that typically appear on the face around the lower eyelids, forehead, or cheeks. Milia occurs when dead skin cells and natural oils become trapped in the skin’s pores. 

There are many causes of milia which include: 
- Improper skin exfoliation can lead to buildup of keratin that can lead to milia
- Cosmetic products such as concealers, foundations, moisturizers that don’t suit your skin type
- Genetics
- Excessive sun exposure can damage the skin leading to to milia

In my practice, I’ve seen a decent amount of patients who are concerned with the appearance of milia. Many times the cause is the use of makeup and/or skincare products that are not suitable for their skin type. Preventing milia involves proper skincare, including regular exfoliation (2-3x a week) and choosing non-comedogenic and suitable cosmetic products for your skin type. 

We can treat milia with a gentle chemical peel, microdermabrasion, or extracting them in office. A consultation is required for me to determine the best treatment option for you.

transcript: This beautiful young woman desired a narrower face, so Shondu went a buckle fat removal. And this is an operation where fat is removed from the cheeks to narrow them. As you can see, she developed a hematoma afterwards on the left side of her face. Well, the hematoma should be in general evacuated to treat it, but if it's not evacuated then, unfortunately, in her case, it ended up getting infected. And this is how she looked like after that. She had to undergo multiple rounds of antibiotics and thank God she is doing much better. But wow, this is a lot to go through. And here she is. After she is healed, you can see she looks great. Hematomas do in general absorb. They can just take a long time for that to happen. Now, buckle fat removal is an operation that I do quite often. And essentially what we do is we make an incision on the inside of the cheek and we tease out that buckle fat. And that is fat basically in your cheek hollows. The idea is this is a natural contouring of the cheek. So going from something like this to something like that. But this is not something that I recommend with somebody who has a thin face because it can skeletonize the face and cause it to look older, especially with age. But in the right patient, it can be a really nice treatment. This is a patient of mine who underwent a lower facelift and a buckle fat removal. As you can see, she looks fantastic afterwards. caption:
Sclerotherapy is a proven, minimally invasive treatment that effectively targets noticeable leg veins, such as spider veins and varicose veins. This non-surgical procedure involves injecting a specialized solution directly into the veins, causing them to collapse and fade away naturally. 

How it works:  The sclerotherapy solution, polidocanol, is injected through tiny needles, targeting the damaged veins. The solution irritates the lining of the vein, causing it to disappear. Over the next few weeks, the treated veins are naturally absorbed in the body, leading to no more leg veins! It’s recommended to have 3 sessions of Sclerotherapy spaced 6 weeks apart for optimal results. These results will last over 2-3 years! 

Benefits of Sclerotherapy include: 

✨ Reduces visible leg veins
✨ Enhances overall skin tone
✨ Quick and painless with no downtime
✨ Safe, FDA approved, and suitable for all skin types
✨ Long lasting results that get better overtime

caption:
Can you spot the melanoma? 👀

Clinically, pigmented lesions can look quite strikingly similar. Dermoscopy helps us recognize subtle clues to melanoma, and earlier detection can improve outcomes. ❤️‍🩹

*Patient consent was obtained. 

*This video is for education only and does not replace medical advice. Consult a dermatologist for any suspicious lesions.

#melanoma #melanomaawareness #skincancer #skincancerawareness #greenscreen 

*Cette vidéo est éducative et ne remplace pas un avis médical. Consultez un dermatologue pour toute lésion suspecte.
on_screen_hook: Which of these four spots is a melanoma? Let's use dermoscopy to
transcript: Which of these four spots is a melanoma? Let's use dermoscopy to figure it out. Lesion 1 is a tiny flat, immensely pigmented, almost jet black macule. The degree of pigmentation can certainly look concerning. Dermoscopy shows a strikingly dark reticular pigment network that is sharply defined and mostly regular and organized, almost as if somebody dropped ink onto the skin. Diagnosis, ink spot lentigo. This one's benign. Lesion 2 is an irregularly shaped, deeply pigmented blue black macule on melanin rich skin, which clinically can certainly raise concern. Dermoscopy reveals a homogeneous structureless blue pigmentation. That blue colour likely represents melanin deeper in the dermis due to the Tyndall effect. Diagnosis: blue nevus. This one's also benign. Lesion 3, another dark, irregularly shaped macule. At First glance this almost looks like a pigment network but if you look closer, this is not a true melanocytic network. These are non melanocytic structures including fissures, ridges, milia like cysts and comedolike openings. Diagnosis, a benign sebaceous keratosis. With a naked eye, lesion 4 already has asymmetry, an irregular border, multiple colours including pink, brown and black and a growing diameter. On dermatoscopy, we can appreciate a true reticular melanocytic network at the periphery along with an architectural disorder, irregular pigmentation, areas of regression, irregular dots and globules, scar like depigmentation and areas of grey peppering. This is a melanoma in situ. Clinically pigmented lesions can look strikingly similar and even an expert eye may need a biopsy to confirm the Diagnosis, but dermoscopy brings us much closer to diagnostic certainty and helps us detect melanoma much earlier among its mimickers.

title: Celebs Caught With Ozempic Face | Then vs Now
transcript: Sharon Osborn lost so much weight that she admitted she could barely recognize her own face. After using Osempic, Sharon said she became too gaunt and even struggled to regain weight. Fans immediately noticed her hollow cheeks, sharper jawline, and dramatic loss of facial volume. One of the most talked about examples of what's now called Osempic face. Then there's Whoopi Goldberg. Whoopi openly admitted she used Monjaro after her weight reached nearly 300 pounds. Her transformation shocked fans, but it also sparked conversations about how rapid weight loss can dramatically change facial appearance. Next is Kathy Bates. Kathy lost around 100 pounds and later explained that while Osempic helped, it wasn't the whole story. Fans immediately noticed her face looked much slimmer with more defined features and less facial volume than before. Then there's Rosie O'Donnell. Rosie revealed she was using Monjaro and said it completely changed her appetite. As the weight came off, fans also noticed a much leaner, more angular appearance compared to previous years. Joy Behar also surprised viewers. After revealing she lost around 25 pounds using Osempic, fans began comparing before and after photos pointing to a noticeably slimmer face alongside her weight loss. And finally, Kelly Osbourne. Kelly has repeatedly denied using Osempic for her weight loss, but her dramatically slimmer appearance has fueled non-stop online speculation. Fans continue debating her transformation every time new photos surface. Even though she has pushed back against the rumors. But here's what most people don't realize. Osempic face isn't actually caused by the medication itself. Doctors say it's the result of rapid weight loss, which can reduce facial fat, making cheeks appear hollow and facial features look more defined or older. The same effect can happen after any significant weight loss, not just with GLP1 medications.

transcript: It's been over three months and you're still purging. That's not purging. In fact, I'd be willing to bet that for 99.999% of you guys it was never purging in the first place. Purging? It's real. It can happen, but it's not as common as the internet would have you believe. Purging refers to the temporary increase in the number of acne spots that you get when you start a topical that increases the rate of skin cell turnover. Typically that would be a retinoid, but in theory it can happen with other things, but in reality it's rare. Importantly, when it does happen, it does not go beyond three months. An increase in acne or continued acne beyond three months is not purging. It's either skin irritation that's worsening the acne, or your acne is not adequately controlled by topical retinoids.

caption:
Not all aesthetic treatments are created equal—and some come with risks that deserve serious consideration.

In this video, Dr. Ariel Ostad shares a concerning case involving AlloClae performed at another practice. The patient developed a severe reaction at the injection site, leading to redness, inflammation, pain, and ultimately an abscess, requiring medical intervention.

Dr. Ostad also addresses a larger issue: he does not recommend AlloClae, citing both safety and ethical concerns. Because it involves injecting fat derived from a cadaver, there is a real risk that the body may recognize it as foreign and mount a significant inflammatory or rejection response, sometimes with serious consequences.

This case underscores an important point: just because a treatment is available doesn’t mean it’s the right choice. Understanding what’s being injected into your body and choosing a highly experienced, board-certified physician can make all the difference in both your results and your safety.

They deliver the energy deep into the facial structure with, again, the promise of lifting and tightening. That's what they're for, right? They're They're supposed to be alternatives to facelift. When these companies and these procedures claim that they can tighten the face or lift the face, etc., they leave a complete wake of unsatisfied and underwhelmed patients. And that is the reason why I don't recommend it. Simply put, be wary of non-surgical treatments in this day and age that attempt to solve a surgical problem, e.g., sagging, with a non-surgical tool. And frankly, honestly, the results are so minimal and almost non-existent, and the risk of causing irreversible fat loss and heating those deep tissues is is high enough. To me, it's mostly downside with very little upside. And if you hear the the claims and the experiences of a lot of people who've used these treatments, they feel that they actually look older and more hollowed-out after starting some of these treatments. Now, obviously, this doesn't happen to everyone who gets a procedure like this, but it happens enough to where you have to be careful between the risk and the benefit, which is always the point here. So, in this case, extremely high risk for very little, if any, reward. Avoid them, in my opinion.

Now don't get me wrong, we use peels all the time in dermatology and we use them safely in skin of color and in fact we can sometimes also use TCA peels in patients of color but what we do is we change the strength of it and so we either decrease the strength and or we're also monitoring it so making sure that we're not getting a degree of frost that's going to cause so much inflammation that could then lead to scarring which is a whole other issue. So we do use peels, we can use them safely and effectively, absolutely not like please just do not do them at home, please please please see a professional because like we know exactly the types of peels that we should be using that we can use that are safe and also I also want to add that some people feel like the more it hurts or the more drastic the peel is the better it works and that is not true, that is not true at all. caption:
🧬 Una vacuna personalizada contra el melanoma acaba de conseguir resultados positivos en fase 3. Y sí, es una noticia muy importante.

Pero hay que contarla bien.

💉 No es una vacuna preventiva que te pones para evitar desarrollar cáncer. Se utiliza en pacientes con melanoma de alto riesgo cuyo tumor ya ha sido extirpado quirúrgicamente.

🔬 Después se analiza el tumor de cada paciente, se identifican características específicas de sus células cancerosas y, con esa información, se fabrica una vacuna de ARN mensajero individualizada. Es decir: cada paciente recibe una vacuna diseñada para su propio tumor.

🛡️ El objetivo es enseñar al sistema inmunitario a reconocer esas señales para que pueda atacar células cancerosas residuales o que vuelvan a aparecer.

La vacuna se administra junto a pembrolizumab, un tratamiento de inmunoterapia, y en el ensayo fase 3 la combinación mejoró significativamente tanto el tiempo sin recaída como el tiempo sin aparición de metástasis frente a utilizar únicamente la inmunoterapia.

👥 El estudio ha incluido a 1.137 pacientes y seis hospitales españoles han participado en él.

⚠️ Eso sí: todavía no conocemos todos los datos completos del fase 3. Por eso, los porcentajes concretos que aparecen en algunos titulares proceden de estudios anteriores y no deberían atribuirse todavía a este nuevo ensayo.

Quedan preguntas importantes sobre aprobación, tiempo de fabricación, precio y acceso. Pero conseguir que una vacuna diseñada específicamente para el tumor de cada paciente funcione en un ensayo fase 3 es, sin duda, un paso enorme para la oncología personalizada.

#Melanoma #Cáncer #ARNm #Inmunoterapia #Oncología Investigación Salud FarmacéuticoFernández
transcript: ¿Os habéis enterado ya de esta buenísima y esperanzadora noticia? Me refiero obviamente a lo del éxito de la primera vacuna contra el melanoma, no a que las empresas haya subido su cotización en bolsa. Pues bien, es una súper noticia porque en el futuro podría revolucionar la eficacia del tratamiento contra uno de los cánceres de piel más agresivos, que es lo que es el melanoma. Porque en realidad no es una vacuna que se utilice para prevenir el cáncer, es una vacuna que se utiliza en personas que ya lo tienen y se les ha estilpado el tumor. Y a partir del análisis de las células tumorales extraídas de ese paciente se diseña una vacuna personalizada, que no es igual para todo el mundo, es específica para ese paciente. Y esa vacuna lo que hace es enseñar el sistema inmunitario a las defensas del paciente las características específicas de su tumor para que si las células cáncerosas vuelven a aparecer enseguida pueda reconocerlas y atacarlas. Y esto lo que consigue reducir la posibilidad de que el cáncer vuelva o incluso de que se produzca metastasis, es decir, que el cáncer se vaya a otras partes del cuerpo aliarla. Lo más importante que esto ya ha funcionado en un ensayo fase 3, que es uno de los últimos pasos antes de que pueda convertirse en un tratamiento de uso real y habitual. Aunque hay que ser realistas, si todos sale bien en salir al mercado todavía tardará unos años. Y además, al ser una tecnología tan puntera que requiere esa personalización es razonable pensar que sería bastante caro. Por lo que tampoco sabemos si los sistemas de salud pública podrían asumir el coste que significaría utilizarlo en todos los pacientes que podrían beneficiarse de ello. Pero bueno, que no quiero yo pinchar el globo de la felicidad porque aún así es un avance enorme. Demuestra que somos capaces de conseguir tratamientos cada vez más personalizados y de enseñarle al sistema inmunitario que es lo que tiene que buscar en cada paciente. Y si consigue llegar a la práctica clínica podría revolucionar la forma en la que tratamos este y otros tipos de cáncer. Y por cierto, seis hospitales españoles han participado en este ensayo.

transcript: Silicone sheets are used in burn units, but pressed onto a healing scar daily, they can help flatten and fade it. Centella asiatica is a trendy Korean skincare ingredient, but it has evidence for wounds healing and reducing inflammation. Bakuchiol is marketed as a natural retinol alternative, but it does not work through the same receptors, so it is not a true substitute if you need real retinoid benefit. Glycerin is one of the most boring ingredients on a label, but it remains one of the most effective humectants studied. Rice water has gone viral for skin brightening, but the evidence behind it is mostly anecdotal, unlike niacinamide or vitamin C. Oatmeal is a breakfast food, but colloidal oatmeal is an FDA recognized skin protectorant that calms eczema and itchy irritated skin.
why: A 'did you know' skincare-facts list opens on a surprising scar fact, though it underperforms with weak delivery.

🩺 „OZEMPIC-Face“ – der neue TREND!
Was steckt wirklich dahinter? 🤓
 Auf Social Media bekannt als die „Wunderspritze fürs Traumgewicht“  ist die Rede vom Diabetes-Medikament Ozempic (Wirkstoff: Semaglutid). 💊 

Entwickelt wurde es zur Behandlung von Typ-2-Diabetes, einer chronischen Stoffwechselerkrankung, bei der die Körperzellen schlechter auf Insulin reagieren und der Blutzucker dauerhaft erhöht ist. Ozempic hilft dabei, den Blutzuckerspiegel zu senken – und als „Nebeneffekt“ verringert es nebenbei auch das Hungergefühl verringern.

Und genau DA da wurde „Hollywood“ aufmerksam 🙃 Denn Menschen ohne medizinische Indikation lassen sich das Medikament off-label verschreiben, um „schnell schlank“ zu werden. 

Und das natürlich nicht ohne Nebenwirkungen:  ➡️ Das Gesicht wird auffällig schmal (Stichwort: Ozempic-Face), denn an welchen Stellen man abnimmt, kann man sich vorher nicht aussuchen ➡️ Es drohen Übelkeit, Durchfall, Muskelschwund 
💡 Wann ist Ozempic sinnvoll? Zum Beispiel  bei Typ-2-Diabetes, wenn Lebensstiländerungen allein nicht mehr reichen. Auch bei starkem Übergewicht mit Begleiterkrankungen kann es als ärztlich begleitete Maßnahme hilfreich sein. ABER: Eine Spritze ersetzt keine gesunde Ernährung, keine Bewegung und schon gar nicht Selbstfürsorge.

The myth that sunscreen causes cancer evolves from  evidence that some chemical sunscreens get absorbed through the skin, and the fact that some batches of (mostly aerosol) sunscreens were contaminated with benzene. This is more of an issue with aerosols and has nothing to do with the sunscreen itself. 
2. It is still possible to tan and get hyperpigmentation/melasma while wearing sunscreen since it doesn’t provide perfect UVA coverage. 
3. Bemotrizinol is the first sunscreen ingredient that’s FDA approved in over 20 years. It provides broad spectrum UV protection, little absorption into the body, and may be more elegant feel/smell than our current US chemical sunscreens. It’s been used in Europe and Asia for decades, and will available in the US under the name PARSOL shields in August. Let me know if you plan to try it. 
#sunscreen #dermatologist
why: A numbered on-screen myth list ('sunscreen doesn't cause cancer') is quick to read and share.

It certainly can be due to injection technique, but every single experienced injector in the best in the world have had several eyelid ptosis and any injector that tells you otherwise is either lying or a brand new injector. However, what does really matter when going to an injector is not to ensure that they've never had any complications occur before because that's actually not a good sign. You want an injector with that kind of experience and knowledge of how to treat those complications if and when they occur, but you want to ensure that your injector is being upfront and transparent on the front end about the risk of complications, what that would look like when you start to see these complications occur and how they would manage them. An eyelid ptosis occurs because neurotoxin diffuses into this levator palpebrae superioris muscle that works to keep the lid open. We know that neurotoxin is an opposite drug, meaning it makes the muscle do the opposite of what it naturally does. So if that muscle naturally keeps the lid open, it makes sense that toxin would do the opposite and try to close that lid, also causing the unaffected eye to work harder and overcompensate and recruit. Now for this muscle that can't work as hard, which is why her other eye, the unaffected side, appears to be bulging or bug eye. And this can happen due to extrusion force, so how quickly the volume in the syringe is being pushed, also the direction of the needle. It typically happens when we're injecting the lateral corrugators. Depth matters if we're too deep, if the needle is directed towards that frame in. So also lying down flat within four hours, exercising within 24 hours, and massaging or manipulating the injection site within four weeks of a tox treatment before it has had a chance to fully settle can all increase the risk of acquiring an eyelid ptosis. So I treated this patient by injecting two units originally in the pre-torsal muscle here. So the pre-torsal muscle is one of the muscles that works to close the lid, meaning it will have the opposite effect and help to open the lid. So then I saw her a week later post pre-torsal injection and I decided to inject four more units into that pre-torsal muscle here and a few more units in the orbicularis oculi muscle. And this was her improvement after one week. And this was her eyelid after two weeks. Here is the side by side in two weeks post ptosis. I always tell my patients this is just always a risk of getting tox in. If you're not okay, well it's not ideal if you're not okay with it and you would have a it would be the end of the world then I don't want to treat you because these are medications and at the end of the day it's just it can happen people have variations in anatomy and I'll always educate you on the front end on how we can help mitigate the risk of them but just know that you do not have to wait three months for an eyelid ptosis to wear off. caption:
Just because a treatment is trending doesn’t mean it’s the right treatment for you.

Sculptra has seen a significant rise in popularity, driven in part by the growing conversation around collagen stimulation and “regenerative” aesthetics.

But trends can oversimplify something that should always be highly individualized.

In aesthetic medicine, the question shouldn’t be “What treatment is everyone getting?” It should be “What is actually causing the change I’m trying to correct?”

Volume loss, skin laxity, texture, and structural changes are not the same—and they shouldn’t automatically be treated the same way.

In this video, Dr. Ostad shares his perspective on the rise of Sculptra, where it can have a role, and why choosing a treatment based on anatomy and long-term goals will always matter more than choosing one based on popularity.

Good aesthetic medicine isn’t about following trends. It’s about knowing when—and when not—to treat.

#Sculptra #AestheticMedicine #CosmeticDermatology #FacialRejuvenation #NaturalResults #ArielOstadMD #NYCDermatologist
transcript: Hi everyone, I wanted to address really my opinion about use of sculpture. Sculpture is having a major moment on social media right now and whenever I see an aesthetic treatment become a trend, I really get concerned. Really your face should never be treated according to what happens to be popular this year. Sculpture is polyelactic acid, which is powdered suture. Unlike a traditional hyaluronic acid filler, it works by creating a tissue response that stimulates your body to produce collagen, but that's really a type of collagen that leads to scarring. That is why precisely I personally take a very conservative approach to using sculpture. We now know that inflammatory reactions, nodules, scarring occur with these bio stimulators like sculpture, but not with hyaluronic acid. We're now having an interesting conversation with facial surgery about what repeated bio stimulatory treatments with sculpture can really eventually lead to issues when someone needs a facelift down the line. Recent survey of facial surgeons found that many report greater difficulty operating on patients who've had sculpture and bio stimulatory treatments such as difficulty dissecting the tissue, longer operating times, changes in planning for surgery. That study wasn't specifically about sculpture alone. It doesn't mean that everyone who has sculpture is going to have a surgical complication, but I think it's something patients deserve to know and something we need to continue studying. I find people who are doing sculpture really at an early age, and what those things are repeatedly with sculpture, you can have problems in your 50s and 60s when it comes to surgical intervention. For me, aesthetic medicine is really about thinking long term down the line. You can choose something that's being injected into your face simply because it's viral. Ask what it does, ask what the potential complications are, ask whether there's an alternative, and most importantly, ask whether you actually need it, rely on a trusted provider who's had years of experience, trends really come and go, but your face deserves a long term plan. So I hope that helps. Thank you.

caption:
Does tretinoin really stop working over time? Dermatologist Dr. Dray explains why your skin becoming more tolerant of tretinoin does not necessarily mean the retinoid has stopped working.

If acne comes back while using tretinoin, there may be other explanations, including changes in hormones, acne severity, skincare routines, or how consistently the medication is being used. Tretinoin and other topical retinoids can also be used as maintenance treatments to help prevent acne from returning.

Dr. Dray breaks down the difference between retinoid tolerance and resistance, and why irritation is not a sign that tretinoin is working better.

title: Why Tretinoin Stops Working
transcript: What's the deal? Why is my tretinoin no longer working? Did my skin become resistant to it? This is something a lot of people end up encountering when it comes to using a topical retinoid. The benefits that they observed in the beginning, maybe they've observed them for a while. All of a sudden, it doesn't cut it in. Your acne, it's breaking out. So does this stop working? No. Topical retinoids do not stop working. Nor does your skin develop tolerance to or resistance against. Topical retinoids work by binding to certain receptors and skin cells and influencing the genes that are expressed, ultimately playing a role in how they act. And that doesn't change with ongoing use. What is more likely is that your skin condition is no longer well controlled by this topical alone. In the case of acne, this is not actually unusual. Acne is influenced by your hormones, which can change throughout your lifetime. It doesn't mean that this stop working. It just means that perhaps you need to see your dermatologist because maybe you need additional treatment in order to now exert control above and beyond a topical retinoid.

caption:
Retinol jest niestabilny. Światło, tlen i wysoka temperatura mogą prowadzić do jego rozkładu. Dlatego przy wyborze produktu najpierw patrzę na opakowanie, a dopiero potem na procent z etykiety. 
2
Opakowanie powinno chronić zawartość przed światłem i ograniczać kontakt z powietrzem. Nieprzezroczysta tubka czy odpowiednio zaprojektowany airless mogą w tym pomagać. Sama ciemna butelka nie daje jednak gwarancji stabilności, a przezroczysta nie jest dowodem, że produkt nie działa.

Perfumy, złoto i lista modnych dodatków też nie powiedzą nam, jak dobrze zabezpieczono retinol. Znaczenie mają przemyślana formuła, antyoksydanty, ewentualna enkapsulacja oraz badania stabilności w docelowym opakowaniu. Liczy się nie tylko to, ile retinolu dodano podczas produkcji, ale również ile pozostaje podczas stosowania.

Właśnie za dopracowaną formulację, opakowanie i kontrolę jakości warto płacić. Wysoka cena sama tego nie gwarantuje.

Ale jest jeszcze jedna kwestia. Produkt reklamowany jako retinol może nie zawierać samego retinolu. Na froncie znajdziesz RETINOL, a w INCI Retinyl Palmitate, bez osobnej pozycji Retinol.

Palmitynian retinylu to nie retinol. To jego ester, czyli inna forma witaminy A. Zanim powstanie z niego kwas retinowy, musi zostać przekształcony w retinol, następnie w retinal i dopiero w kwas retinowy. Wyników badań nad samym retinolem nie możemy automatycznie przypisywać produktowi z jego estrem. 

Nie oznacza to, że taki kosmetyk nie daje żadnych efektów. Oznacza, że stosujesz inną substancję. A 1% palmitynianu retinylu nie jest tym samym co 1% retinolu.

Zanim uznasz, że retinol nie działa, sprawdź, co właściwie nakładasz.
#retinol #retinolserum

La femme adulte qui présente de l'acné doit aller voir en dermatologue car la cause peut être dû au SMOP, anciennement appelé SOPK. Le syndrome métabolique ovarien-poli-endocrinien, anciennement SOPK, peut entraîner de l'acné, de l'hersuitisme, c'est-à-dire des poils au niveau de la barbe chez la femme et une perte de cheveux, avec bien sûr d'autres signes qui peuvent être retrouvés comme une résistance à l'insuline. Il existe plusieurs stades d'acné avec le stade le moins sévère qui se traite avec des produits d'hygiène et des produits de soins. Au stade les plus sévères qui se traite avec de l'iso-tritinoïne ou parfois avec des anti-androgène ou d'autres produits équivalents. C'est pour cela qu'il est préférable de venir consulter chez le dermatologue pour connaître la cause de votre acné et avoir le traitement le plus adapté à votre situation.

Then we use fluorescence imaging, which lights up the damaged sites inside. After 10 uses, There was 65% fewer damage sites in Caucasian hair and 54% fewer in afro textured hair. So it was cutting deep into the cortex and repairing the damage, not just coating the surface. Seeing the data match what our testers was telling us meant everything to me. Una de las cosas más frustrantes de la rosácea es su carácter fluctuante: períodos de calma y brotes que aparecen sin causa aparente, con el mismo tratamiento.

Hay una observación que vale la pena mirar de cerca. Los disparadores clásicamente descritos para la rosácea —alcohol, quesos estacionados, comidas picantes, embutidos, exposición al calor— se superponen de manera notable con los alimentos y situaciones asociados a mayor carga de histamina.

Y existe respaldo mecanístico: se ha demostrado que los mastocitos, las células que almacenan y liberan histamina, son mediadores clave en la inflamación cutánea iniciada por catelicidina en la rosácea. La densidad de mastocitos en la piel afectada está aumentada..

Lo que sí puede plantearse es que comparten un actor común —el mastocito y la histamina que libera— y que en algunas personas la carga de histamina podría comportarse como un factor modulador de la intensidad de los brotes.

Cuánta histamina puede degradar tu organismo depende de tus variantes genéticas en AOC1 (DAO), HNMT y las vías de metilación. Es una variable individual y medible.

Si tenés rosácea que fluctúa sin explicación clara, evaluar esa vía puede aportar información que el tratamiento dermatológico solo no contempla.

caption:
Why does retinol keep wrecking your skin? Comment RETINOL for the full progression and how to know when to move up. This is not a ranking. It’s a route.

THE RULE: your skin can only use one form of vitamin A — retinoic acid. Everything else has to convert first.

Retinol needs TWO conversion steps. Retinaldehyde needs ONE. Tretinoin needs NONE, because it already is retinoic acid.

That’s why retinal is roughly 10x the strength of the same percentage of retinol, and why retinol is around 20x weaker than tretinoin. Every step up this stand is one less conversion your skin has to do.

START HERE — bottom tier

Neutrogena retinol cream. Haru Haru Wonder retinol at 0.08%, formulated alongside ceramides and bakuchiol — genuinely gentle and a sensible first bottle. Then Neutrogena or L’Oreal serum at 0.3%.

Stay here 8–12 weeks minimum. If you’re not irritated, you are not failing. You’re building tolerance, which is the entire point.

STEP UP — middle tier

The Ordinary 0.5%, Sunday Riley A+, Paula’s Choice retinol. Same molecule, more of it.

Then the encapsulated retinals. Celimax at 0.2% and Amahvas Ocean of Milk at 0.1%. Retinal is the stronger molecule, but encapsulation slows the release — stronger active, gentler delivery. Amahvas pairs its 0.1% with a 2.5% PHA blend rather than stacking harsher acids, and skips fragrance entirely. It is the best-built bridge on this stand.

TOP TIER — only if the previous step has stopped yielding results. 

The Ordinary Retinal 0.2%, unencapsulated. Nothing slowing it down.

And at the end, compounded tretinoin. No conversion, no waiting — it is retinoic acid. That is a prescription conversation with a doctor, not a shopping decision, and I’m deliberately not giving you strengths.

You don’t win at retinol by starting strong. You win by still using it in year three.

#retinol #retinal #tretinoin #skincarescience #skincareeducator

Sclerotherapy is a proven, minimally invasive treatment that effectively targets noticeable leg veins, such as spider veins and varicose veins. This non-surgical procedure involves injecting a specialized solution directly into the veins, causing them to collapse and fade away naturally.

How it works: The sclerotherapy solution, polidocanol, is injected through tiny needles, targeting the damaged veins. The solution irritates the lining of the vein, causing it to disappear. Over the next few weeks, the treated veins are naturally absorbed in the body, leading to no more leg veins! It’s recommended to have 3 sessions of Sclerotherapy spaced 6 weeks apart for optimal results. These results will last over 2-3 years!

✨ Reduces visible leg veins

✨ Quick and painless with no downtime
✨ Safe, FDA approved, and suitable for all skin types
✨ Long lasting results that get better overtime

caption:
The truth about hyaluronic acid fillers 🧬

Recently, hyaluronic acid (HA) fillers have received some negative attention — but it’s important to understand that when performed correctly, fillers remain one of the safest and most effective treatments for facial rejuvenation.

HA fillers are designed to restore lost volume, smooth fine lines and wrinkles, and enhance facial structure — such as defining the jawline or addressing a receding chin. The results and safety of the procedure depend largely on:
✅ The type of filler selected for your specific area and concern
✅ The technique and experience of your injector
✅ Proper placement and dosing tailored to your anatomy

When these elements are done right, the outcome is subtle, natural, and rejuvenating — not overfilled or artificial.

For those who prefer a more regenerative option, PRFM (Platelet-Rich Fibrin Matrix) can be a great alternative. PRFM uses your own platelets and growth factors to stimulate collagen production, improve skin texture, and restore volume gradually — without synthetic fillers.

Both treatments can deliver excellent, natural-looking results when performed by a skilled professional.

Not sure which is right for you? Book your consultation with Dr Ostad by calling (212) 517-7900.
title: Hyaluronic Acid Fillers and PRFM Explained | Safe, Natural Results with Dr Ariel Ostad

But what causes them, and how can you prevent them? Let's break it down! 👇

🦠 Clogged Pores — Whiteheads form when excess oil (sebum) and dead skin cells become trapped inside a pore.

🤍 Trapped Beneath the Skin — Unlike blackheads, whiteheads remain covered by a thin layer of skin, keeping the clogged material from being exposed to air.

💧Excess Oil Production — Increased sebum production can contribute to clogged pores and whitehead formation.

🌿 Dead Skin Cell Buildup — When dead skin cells don't shed properly, they can mix with oil and block pores.

✨How to Help Prevent Whiteheads — Use a gentle cleanser, choose non-comedogenic skincare products, and consider ingredients like salicylic acid to help unclog pores.

💖 Where Niacinamide Helps — Niacinamide can support your skin barrier and may help balance excess oil, making it a useful addition to an acne-prone skincare routine.

📌 Save this reel to understand what's happening beneath your skin!

💡 Pro Tip: Avoid squeezing whiteheads! It can increase irritation, inflammation, and the risk of scarring. Consistent skincare is more effective than aggressive scrubbing.

title: How to get rid of DEEP acne scars?
transcript: If you have these deep scars in your skin, you might think you can just scrub them away. Please don't, because these aren't just dog spots or marks. They're actually acne scars called atrophic scars, meaning it's underneath your skin. This usually happens when you have a deep inflamed pimple and your skin doesn't make enough collagen while it heals. So when the pimple goes away, your skin underneath can sink in, leaving you with a dent in your skin. Now you don't want to treat the acne scars if you're still breaking out, because you're trying to fix the damage while your skin is still creating more. Instead, you want to get your acne under control first. And you can start with a topical retinoid, because this helps prevent new breakouts and post-acne marks. And when you're left with the deep scars, a dermatologist can help with precise treatments, such as chemical peels, subsision, or laser research.

title: What To Know Before Getting A CO2 Laser Skin Treatment
transcript: CO2 and erbium lasers are really powerful, game-changing lasers that I get asked about a lot. And the reason why, in general, they're so powerful is because think of them almost like a lawnmower. Think of it as as your skin being the, you know, the lawn and these ablative CO2 and erbium wavelengths are coming through and removing a portion of the top layer of the skin. So, with it goes the stratum corneum, which is that dull layer of dead surface skin. Then comes the epithelium, the top layer of the skin that sometimes fine lines and wrinkles show up at, pigmentation shows up, and it even can go as deep as the upper portion of the dermis. So, what you do in response to that laser is you're getting a whole new layer of skin that flourishes and grows through. So, this total skin resurfacing that you get by removing those outer layers gives you an all-around rejuvenation. Wrinkles, discoloration, and even texture. The downside, there is always a catch, right? So, you're going to get this beautiful rejuvenation, skin's going to look amazing. The downside is that it A, it's not permanent, although it is definitely longer-lasting. I mean, by the time those deep lines around the top lip starts to reform, it could be literally years if maybe it's a one-and-done even. And if you use proper skin care on top of it after you get this done, a lot of the changes are going to persist because you've gotten this massive momentum shift going forward with this ablative laser. Now, the catch is, unfortunately, they're generally expensive. They have a significant downtime associated with it, anywhere from a week to 3 weeks. And if you are getting this done by somebody who doesn't really know what they're doing, huge huge risk because there's a risk of burning, there's a risk of discoloration, hypopigmentation, a number of other things. So, this is a procedure that you want to get done by an experienced surgeon or dermatologist. This is not a med spa procedure that should be done, generally speaking, by, say a nurse or an aesthetician, etc. So, again, overall game-changing procedure for the right person with the advanced sign of skin aging, but it requires a serious commitment both to healing and finding an expert provider.

Discover Sclerotherapy: A Safe Solution for Leg Veins 🦵🏼

Sclerotherapy is a proven, minimally invasive treatment that effectively targets noticeable leg veins, such as spider veins and varicose veins. This non-surgical procedure involves injecting a specialized solution directly into the veins, causing them to collapse and fade away naturally. 

How it works:  The sclerotherapy solution, polidocanol, is injected through tiny needles, targeting the damaged veins. The solution irritates the lining of the vein, causing it to disappear. Over the next few weeks, the treated veins are naturally absorbed in the body, leading to no more leg veins! It’s recommended to have 3 sessions of Sclerotherapy spaced 6 weeks apart for optimal results. These results will last over 2-3 years! 

Benefits of Sclerotherapy include: 

✨ Reduces visible leg veins

✨Quick and painless with no downtime
✨ Safe, FDA approved, and suitable for all skin types

A liquid facelift, also referred to as a non-surgical facelift, is a cosmetic procedure designed to rejuvenate and enhance the appearance of your facial features without an invasive surgery. This approach combines the use of hyaluronic acid fillers to address various signs of aging, providing a more youthful appearance by restoring volume, reducing wrinkles, and improving overall facial contours. Results from hyaluronic acid fillers can last up to 2 years. 

Another alternative to a facelift we use in my practice is a fat transfer.  For patients that lack volume in the facial area, we can extract fat from areas such as the abdomen or outer thighs then inject into the hollow areas in the face. This procedure provides natural looking, long lasting results. It’s a safe, non-allergenic way to recontour the face and add definition for a long lasting result. These results can last many years  and is a cost effective way to treat major volume loss. I perform this procedure under local anesthesia, which is the best technique to ensure our patients have a safe and speedy recovery with optimal results. 

With both of these treatments, you are able to see immediate results that gradually get better over time. They are both customizable treatments with minimal discomfort and are not as invasive as a facelift.

transcript: When I'm assessing a patient for hyaluronic acid injectables, I always begin by looking at the face, both at rest and in motion. Today, we're looking specifically at the nasolabial folds or laugh lines. It's the lines that extend from the sides of the nose towards the corners of the mouth. We're going to be treating them with Everlice. It's a hyaluronic acid injectable designed to correct moderate to severe dynamic facial wrinkles such as the nasolabial folds. So this is clearly what we're seeing at rest. You have some lines. At rest, I'm looking at the depth of the fold, the contour of the area, and whether there are any natural differences between the two sides of the face. But go ahead and just smile now, animate, okay. We want to make sure that when you do like smile, like some of these lines are not as obvious. This is an important part of my assessment because the face isn't static. As she smiles, I can see how these folds change with movement and where they become more pronounced. Relax again and smile one more time, perfect. When I'm assessing this area, I'm not simply looking at whether a line exists. I'm looking at its depth, how it changes with expression, the differences between each side and how it relates to the patient's natural facial movement. Everly smooth and Everly's form are hyaluronic acid injectables that can be used to correct moderate to severe dynamic facial wrinkles, including the nasolabial folds. Here we're using a softer product which is called Everly Smooth. What's nice about Everly Smooth is it's finer. We use it for fine lines. It will make such a nice difference. Which product I select and how I approach treatment depends on what I see during the individual patient's assessment. One of the most important things with hyaluronic acid injectables is knowing when enough is enough. My goal isn't to completely erase every fold or change the way someone's face naturally moves. These folds are part of the normal facial anatomy and expression. So instead I'm looking for areas where thoughtful correction can soften one's appearance while respecting the patient's natural features. So it's all about proportions. It's about customizing the treatment to each patient without really over-filling you so that you walk out of here and people see you and they're like, wow, you look great. What did you do? That tells me a great deal about how I want to approach the treatment. The injection itself is really only one part of the process. For me, the assessment is what creates the treatment plan and understanding the anatomy, observing the face in motion and deciding how much correction is appropriate for that individual patient.

transcript: Every year when November rolls around, I get tons of messages about how to optimise your residency application. I've been in the game for nearly a decade. I started medical school in 2015. I matched around COVID, then finished my intern year and dermatology residency, and I've been an attending for a few years. I've been a medical student on the other side, but I've also sat on admissions committees and tutored other students going through the same process. So if you wanna listen to me, these are my top three tips that I give every single one of my students and why I think I was successful in terms of the match. Number one, mentorship is the most important thing. Think about it very intuitively here. A mentor will give you a sense of the field, but the most important thing is that they're going to advocate for you. They can put you in touch with colleagues for rotations or research. They have a sense of what different programs entail, community versus academic. And hopefully they will pick up the phone when someone calls about who you are as an applicant. Mentorship is the most important thing, I will say. Absolutely, hands down. Especially when it comes to dermatology. Second thing I'll say is just commit to something. I would much rather take a student who has shown an interest long term in something, even if they ended up changing their mind later, rather than bouncing around many different fields and doing one project here or there. So, for example, this could be starting a club, working with a non profit, doing research. Show that you are doing something over time and building yourself within that role. It's going to pay off even if you don't end up doing that field, because it just shows that you can get the job done. Tip No. 3. Do something different. So, yes, I had the grades, I had the research. Like, not to brag, but I had, like, 25 publications going into residency applications. But guess what came up more than any of those things. Nothing to do with medicine. It was actually about fashion design. So before I started medical school, I actually studied fashion design and ended up getting a degree in it. This came up way, way more than my research or my grades because it was different, and it showed that I could use a different part of my brain and commit to something. Hands down, this came up on every single interview I went on. Those are my big three. Mentorship, commit to something, and do something different. title: Skin Barrier Routine
transcript: I'm a derm PA and this is the best routine for a damaged skin barrier. Signs to look out for include dryness, tightness, redness, stinging, burning, maybe small kind of rash-like bumps, and suddenly reacting to products that you used to be able to tolerate. This can be triggered from skin conditions like perioral dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, or maybe eczema. But most of the time it's from overdoing it with skin care. You really need to pause everything and go back to the basics. a moisturizer, and a sunscreen. Plus one extra product I tell my patients to use that can make the biggest difference. If you just push through damaged skin barrier, that's going to accumulate a lot of irritation, which can then turn into red spots and dark marks that are a lot harder to fade than you think. For cleansing, if you're wearing makeup or water-resistant sunscreen, then you want to make sure it's fully off with the proper products. You can either go for micellar water, which you typically don't have to rinse off, or you can go for an oil-based cleanser as the first step in a double cleanse routine. And then for your regular cleanser, I recommend going for a non-foaming or very low-foaming formula. These types of cleansers are the least likely to strip your skin barrier any further than you're already dealing with. Some non-foaming cleansers are going to feel like you're applying lotion to your skin, but don't worry because it's still cleaning your skin and doing its job, just very gentle. For moisturizer, you want to use one that your skin already loves, or find one with ingredients that are going to help rebuild and calm your skin. You can look for oats in moisturizers, or you can look for ceramides, niacinamide, centella, panthenol. Those are all great ingredients to help support your skin barrier. Also, you want to apply it to damp skin after cleansing, unless it stings, then you want to do dry skin. And every single morning, no matter what, you have to wear your sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher. If it's irritating your skin, then check the ingredients because sometimes chemical sunscreens can be more irritating when you have a damaged skin barrier. So, in that case, you want to go for mineral-based sunscreens. These have zinc oxide or titanium dioxide, and these are a lot more gentle on the skin. Or, you can also go for authentic Korean skin care sunscreens because these use more gentle chemical filters compared to the ones we currently have. Now, the extra product is incorporating a partial or full occlusive at night on top of your moisturizer. Partial occlusives are like healing balms including Cicaplast and Cicaplast, and full occlusives are petrolatum-based. When your barrier is damaged, it can't hold on to water, so it's constantly losing moisture, and that's what keeps your skin irritated. An occlusive is what locks that moisture back in, and in literature, it does more than just hydrate your skin. Because once your skin stops losing water, that's the signal that tells it to start repairing itself. Now, you know the best routine to heal your damaged skin barrier, and follow me for more tips from a dermatologist.

transcript: Here's an update and a brief recap of my basal cell carcinoma journey. I've had this spot on my nose for decades. My dermatologist at the time somehow missed it. I now have a new dermatologist and he did a biopsy. It's a nodular basal cell on my alar, this part of the nose right here. I was told I had two options, Mohs surgery or superficial radiation. A surgical appointment was immediately set for Mohs. But I asked to have a consultation first. I spoke to the Mohs surgeon who also does SRT, superficial radiation. I asked him for an ultrasound to see the tumor before I decided, but he declined. And in case I did choose radiation, he sent me to a different radiologist. He also suggested a plastic surgeon for reconstruction in case I do Mohs. I saw the radiologist he recommended and I asked him if I could have an ultrasound prior to treatment. So I could decide on treatment method. But he also declined saying, well, you really can't see that much. Then I had an appointment with the plastic surgeon. He showed me photos of the paramedial flap on the forehead. And he drew an example of how that paramedial flap works as we were speaking. That scared me. Then when I told the Mohs surgeon I needed more time to think about it, he sent out a letter saying I had declined treatment, which wasn't so. After that, I found a facility on my own which does high frequency ultrasounds, HFUS. Thankfully, my dermatologist agreed to order one for me. He also set up an appointment with a different Mohs surgeon for a second opinion. I now have the shape and measurements of the tumor and most importantly, it doesn't attach to the cartilage. And since I wasn't allowed to take a photograph of the ultrasound image, I drew a picture of it from memory. This is the top layer of the skin. This is the tumor. And down here somewhere is the cartilage. So this week, I had my appointment with a new Mohs surgeon. I showed her the results of the HFUS. And we discussed all treatment options, pros and cons. This is where I broke down and cried because I felt heard. We also discussed alternative treatments, which she did not recommend. So she and I agreed that I would see her again in three months, which should give me enough time to experiment with one or two alternatives, after which time we could evaluate with another HFUS since I have a baseline. So that's where I am. I've started to try castor oil and frankincense. Thank you all so much for your prayers. They are working. I love you to your health.

But in my 30s, I thought it was absolutely a useless treatment because I didn't see a dramatic overnight change. And now at 42, I wish I appreciated microneedling more. And that is the whole point of microneedling. It is a long term game. So this is where I think people are missing the point where they are constantly traumatizing their skin every month getting a microneedling treatment and simply inflaming their skin, which is counter productive. So if you are in your 30s, I would cap out my microneedling sessions to maximum three to four times a year and most definitely not a monthly treatment. But PRP is a slightly different story. So PRP stands for platelet rich plasma, is derived from your blood and it is not a home run for everybody. One way I like to think about Purepe is that it's a fertilizer that's gonna have growth factors that can help and repair and improve your skin quality only if your environment allows it to. So not everyone's going to see a meaningful difference. And personally, I much prefer injecting PRP into your skin rather than simply applying it on top. But before you sign yourself, Up for years of PRP. I would tell you do a series of three treatments spaced one month apart and have it injected in an area where you see the biggest difference, like your under eyes. And make sure to take a shit ton of pictures, but give it time. So after the third treatment, wait two to three months to really see if you see a meaningful difference and to see if it's worth continuing. Ellacor, for those of you who do not know, is basically a micro-coring treatment. Micro-coring means that under local anesthesia, little tiny cores of skin are actually removed. caption:
Me incomoda profundamente ver cómo muchas veces, cuando una persona empieza a cuestionar procedimientos estéticos modernos o comparte experiencias reales sobre sus consecuencias, la respuesta inmediata es atacarla o invalidarla en lugar de abrir conversaciones más honestas. 

Y esto también nos deja una enseñanza muy importante como pacientes: no podemos asumir automáticamente que todo lo nuevo es completamente seguro solo porque está normalizado o porque muchas personas lo hacen. La realidad es que muchas veces las consecuencias reales aparecen años después, cuando ya millones de personas fueron expuestas. 

Hoy incluso existen estudios y debates médicos cuestionando cuánto tiempo permanecen realmente ciertos fillers en el tejido y cómo algunos procedimientos que se vendían como “temporales” o “fácilmente reversibles” son mucho más complejos de lo que se pensaba. 

No creo que todo profesional actúe desde la mala intención, pero sí creo que vivimos en un sistema donde muchas veces el interés económico, las tendencias y la presión estética avanzan más rápido que la investigación a largo plazo. Por eso es tan importante aprender a investigar, cuestionar y tomar decisiones desde la conciencia y no solamente desde el marketing o la validación social. 

Tu cuerpo merece información completa, no solamente la parte bonita del procedimiento.

transcript: Te dijeron que el ácido hielorónico se reabsorbía o que si algo salía mal te lo disolvían, pero eso es una mentira. Cuando publiqué mi vídeo del ácido hielorónico, muchos médicos estéticos vinieron a decirme que yo estaba desinformando, que el problema no es el producto que en manos de profesionales todo es seguro, y que si algo sale mal te inyectan hieloronidasa y eso se disuelve y listo. Eso es falso, y no lo digo yo, lo dice la evidencia científica a la que ustedes tanto se refieren, una evidencia que salió en el 2026. El ácido hielorónico que te inyectan no es el ácido que produce tu cuerpo, es una versión modificada químicamente, se llama ácido hielorónico reticulado. Diseñado específicamente para que ni tu sistema ni la hieloronidasa lo puedan degradar fácilmente, por eso dura meses. Por eso no se va, no se reabsorbe en migra, se desplaza dentro de tu tejido, se acumula y se expande porque atrae agua, y en algunos casos tu cuerpo lo encapsula porque no sabe qué hacer con él. La hieloronidasa, el famoso antídoto, fue redefinida en estudios recientes, ya no se considera un disolvente, se considera un modificante. Lo que más puede hacer es suavizar el relleno para remoldearlo, pero los años que ese tejido vivió con eso que es antinatural, eso no se revierte. Una profesional en técnica de resonancia magnética me confirmó en mis comentarios que el filler genera tanto artefacto en el cuerpo que a veces tiene que suspender el estudio. Eso no es un problema de calidad del producto, eso es lo que le pasa al tejido cuando tiene algo que no debería de estar ahí, y no es solamente el ácido hielorónico, la hidroxapatita cálcica, el ácido poliláctico, todos los inductores de colágeno que se venden como temporales. La evidencia científica muestra que tampoco se va del todo y dejan huella en el tejido. Back with another very commonly asked question, something we see every day in my practice: how to treat rosacea.

#rosacea #dermatologist #skincare #facecare
title: How to Treat Rosacea
transcript: Rosacea is a condition where we see redness on the face, usually central facial redness, so around the nose, forehead, chin, and it can be accompanied with acne bumps as well. And there are considered to be four types of rosacea. There's the erythematotelangiectatic type, which is just straight up redness, and then there's the papulopustular rosacea, so the rosacea that gets a lot of acne bumps associated with it. There's ocular rosacea, so you can get rosacea in your eyes, and then there's something called rhinophyma, where people get like a buildup of sebaceous tissue in their nose. like pretty big noses. When it comes to just basic skin care with rosacea, the main thing is just keeping things gentle. Gentle cleansers, gentle moisturizers, gentle sunscreens. I recommend mineral-based sunscreens over chemical sunscreens. Brands that I really like that have gentle cleansing ingredients are CeraVe, La Roche-Posay, Avène, and Aveeno, as well as their moisturizers.
