The “discovery” genre reveals how thoroughly Eurocentric beauty ideals have colonised collective visual literacy. 

When Indian women trend for being “baddies” at a Tyla concert, it’s framed as discovery rather than recognition, as if we materialised into desirability instead of existing outside the narrow aperture of mainstream media all along.

Here’s what nobody’s saying: the “baddie” framework, borrowed from Black women’s vernacular then flattened, frames being hot as radical self-actualisation. But for women of colour, it’s worth asking who profits when our resistance looks like participation in beauty culture’s most intensive demands.

As a beauty brand, we feel a huge responsibility to curate aspiration beyond aesthetics. Your body can grow life, fight disease, create art, organise movements, and survive what tried to break it. Being attractive was never supposed to be the ceiling.

The project isn’t begging for inclusion in someone else’s beauty metrics. It’s dismantling the frameworks that make beauty a zero-sum game, a colonial inheritance we keep renovating rather than razing.

So when the next viral post “discovers” that [insert ethnicity] women are beautiful: 

What visual world have you been inhabiting that this comes as news? 

And what would it mean to build one where no one’s humanity requires discovery at all?

At L’ORIENT, we are not here to make you acceptable, more beautiful, more palatable. We’re just here so luxury care assumes your belonging as baseline, so you can focus on actually just living in your body.

caption:
A new chapter in melanoma treatment is emerging.

Recent Phase 3 results surrounding a personalized mRNA melanoma vaccine have generated significant attention—and for good reason. But what does a “melanoma vaccine” actually mean?

In this video, Dr. Ostad explains what this new research means, why it matters, and why knowing your skin remains as important as ever.

Unlike a traditional vaccine, this investigational therapy is not designed to prevent someone from developing melanoma. Instead, it is created for certain patients who have already had a high-risk melanoma surgically removed, with the goal of helping the immune system recognize the cancer and reduce the risk of recurrence or spread.

It’s an exciting glimpse into the future of personalized medicine. But even as treatment advances, our most important tools remain the ones we have today: prevention and early detection.

Daily sun protection, regular skin examinations, and paying attention to new or changing spots can make an enormous difference—particularly because melanoma is highly treatable when detected early.

#Melanoma #MelanomaAwareness #SkinCancerAwareness #SkinCancerPrevention #Dermatology #SkinHealth #EarlyDetection #ArielOstadMD
transcript: Hi, everyone. I wanted to just spend a couple of minutes about yesterday's results in the news, about how there is a melanoma vaccine that is now available. It's incredibly exciting, but I just wanted to spend a couple of minutes and break it down. This is not a melanoma vaccine that prevents melanoma, like a typical, let's say, flu vaccine or other vaccines that are given during childhood. So it's not that. It's not a vaccine that will prevent melanoma from ever forming in a patient. However, it is a vaccine that's used in advanced melanoma cases in cases where there is an increased risk of melanoma either recurring or spreading potentially later on to other organs or lymph nodes. So in the past, there were immunotherapy treatments such as Keytruda that basically have been shown to increase survival by reducing the chance of the cancer spreading or coming back. But now there is, in addition to immunotherapy, a melanoma vaccine by Moderna that basically is a personalized mRNA vaccine. And basically the way it works is that once someone has a melanoma that's high risk for coming back or spreading, it's that melanoma studied for specific gene mutations. And then a vaccine is actually developed to target that specific mutation in that patient's melanoma. So it's an exciting personalized vaccine that's developed for each patient depending on their mutation. And the combination of immunotherapy and that vaccine in phase three trials has been shown to actually reduce recurrence or spread by anywhere from 49 to 59%. The data still hasn't completely been published to truly see if actually prolonged survival. But it's incredibly promising that these are patients that will tend to have a disease-free survival for many more years. So it's really exciting news. Hopefully this will be approved in 2027. But I just wanted to tell you the good news. It's really mainly targeted towards patients who have advanced melanoma, basically where there's a higher risk of it spreading or coming back. It's not a vaccine that prevents melanoma. Thank you.

You can use a mirror or ask a friend or partner to check areas that you can't see. Melanomas often an uneven shape. They may have two different shaped halves and uneven edges. caption:
There has been a growing trend, particularly among plastic surgeons, of criticizing dermal filler and pointing to overfilled faces as evidence that patients should abandon injectables in favor of surgery.

I understand where some of that criticism comes from.

For years, aesthetic medicine went through an era where nearly every sign of aging seemed to have the same answer: add more volume. Cheeks, temples, jawlines, lips—every hollow became something to fill.

But when filler is repeatedly added without reassessing the patient's anatomy, it can create heaviness, distorted proportions and an unnatural appearance.

That’s a problem with how filler is being used—not filler itself.

As both a dermatologist and surgeon, I don’t see filler and surgery as opposing philosophies. They are different tools designed to accomplish different things.

A facelift can reposition descended tissue and address significant laxity in a way filler cannot. But strategically placed filler can restore support, improve proportion and subtly balance the face without surgery.

The question shouldn’t be, “Filler or surgery?”

It should be, “What is actually causing the change we’re seeing?”

Sometimes the answer is filler. Sometimes it’s a laser or another technology. Sometimes it’s surgery. And sometimes, the right answer is to do nothing.

That’s also why I don’t believe in treating filler as a commodity.

Faces don’t come in syringes.

Every patient has different anatomy, volume loss, skin quality and goals. Treatment should follow the anatomy—not a predetermined number of syringes or a social media trend.

I welcome the conversation around overfilling. But swinging the pendulum from “filler for everything” to “filler is bad” is another oversimplification.

Natural-looking aesthetic medicine isn’t about filler vs. surgery.

It’s about having the judgment—and restraint—to know when to use each.

— Dr. Ariel Ostad

For years, we saw an era of static medicine where almost every sign of aging was treated by adding more volume, bigger cheeks, sharper jaw lines, fuller lips, filling every hollow, but filler was never really designed to fix everything. transcript: When I assess a patient for neurotoxin treatment, I don't begin by looking at individual wrinkles. I begin by looking at the face as a whole. Every muscle has a function and many of these muscles work in opposition to one another. So before deciding where to treat, I want to understand how the patient's face moves naturally. Let's start with the upper face. Raise your eyebrows for me. So that's from movement of a muscle called the frontalis, which gives you the ability to raise your eyebrow. That's what over time leads to these horizontal lines across your forehead. This is an area where we want to under treat actually. Treatment should always take the patient's individual anatomy and movement into consideration. So now give me a big smile. I'm looking at how far those lines extend, how strong the contraction is, and whether the movement is symmetrical from one side to the other. Because as people smile, some wrinkles form here too, so it actually smooths that area as well. Now I'm going to look at the lower face. Here we're seeing the activity of the depressorangular aris, otherwise known as the DAO. This muscle pulls down the corners of the mouth. In appropriately selected patients, neurotoxin can be used off-label to reduce some of that downward muscular pull. Now, clench your teeth for me. Here I can feel the masseter muscle contracting. The masseter is a very powerful muscle involved in chewing. Neurotoxin treatment of the masseter is another off-label application and may be considered in certain patients depending on their anatomy and treatment goals. So now wrinkle your chin for me. Here we're looking at the mentalist muscle. When this muscle contracts strongly, some patients develop this dimpled or textured appearance across the chin. Neuromodulators can also be used off-label in this area to temporarily reduce that muscular activity and soften its appearance. What I want patients to understand is that neuromodulator treatment isn't simply about chasing individual lines. The forehead, the eyes, the brows, mouth, chin, and jaw all contribute to the way a face moves and expresses itself. So ultimately, I want my patients to still look like themselves. And the goal isn't to eliminate expression altogether, it's to use our understanding of facial anatomy, therefore maintain that natural movement and balance.

caption: Is your Botox no longer working? There may be a reason for that… #botox #dermatologist #dysport #skincare
on_screen_hook: If someone comes in and they think that their Botox is not
transcript: If someone comes in and they think that their Botox is not working as well as it used to, these are four things that I think about. First, there could have been a potential discrepancy with that batch of Botox, the way that it was diluted or handled. We don't like neurotoxin, whether it's Botox, Dysport, Xiamin, Jeuveau. We don't want them to sit at room temperature for prolonged periods of time. It can affect the efficacy of the neurotoxin. Sometimes if the dilution is slightly off, that can affect the potency of the neurotoxin. There is the occasional bad batch where the potency is a little bit different. That's very uncommon. Second is that person maybe just needs more Botox. For those people whose muscles do get stronger, they sometimes do need a gradual increase in some of their Botox amounts. And then third, sort of related to what I just said, is that we are also actively aging. Wrinkles are also getting deeper. The rate at which the wrinkles are getting deeper could be faster than what Botox is able to do for your face. So there could be that. And then fourth, this is super, super rare, but you can become immune or develop what are called neutralizing antibodies against the neurotoxin itself. Like I said, rare. Under 1% of people get this. Overall, Botox or any of the neurotoxins are very helpful, very consistent. These situations can happen, but not so often.

I'm a dermatologist, I specialize in hair and if your scalp gets greasy while your ends are still dry, rough or damaged, then the hair sandwich method is one trend that I actually rate. It's basically when you apply conditioner, shampoo followed by conditioner. And the reason why it can work is because your scalp and your ends don't have the same need. Your scalp is where you're dealing with oil, sweat, dead skin cells, product build up. That is where shampoo actually needs to do its job. But your ends are actually the oldest part of your hair. They've had the most brushing, heat, colouring, which means that your cuticle can be more damaged and the hair can lose moisture more easily. This is exactly how you're gonna nail the sandwich hair method. So before you shampoo, take a small amount of conditioner through your mid lengths to ends. The first layer coats the hair fibre, gives you more slip, and helps reduce friction while washing so your dry ends aren't getting unnecessarily roughed up whilst you're trying to clean your scalp. Then shampoo the scalp properly. You do not need to aggressively scrub shampoo through your ends for a normal wash. The lather running through them When you rinse is more than enough. Then you're gonna finish with your conditioner again. To bring back softness, slip, and manageability after cleansing. This is especially useful if your hair is damaged. But if your hair is fine, that could weigh it down easily. Or you can have lots of build up so you won't need sandwich. Every wash, your scalp and your ends are allowed to need different things.

title: Dr. Ariel Ostad: Why Technique Matters
transcript: One of the most important things that I tell patients about injectables is the product is only one part of the result. Technique truly matters. Two physicians can use the same product on the same area of the face and approach that treatment very differently. Because every face is different. Before I inject anything, I'm studying the patient's anatomy. I'm also thinking about what's underneath the surface. With a neural modulator, really technique begins with understanding facial and muscle anatomy and movement. It's really not simply about seeing a line and injecting it. I want to understand which muscle is creating that movement, how strong that muscle is, how it interacts with the surrounding muscles. The placement of an injection, the dose, the patient's individual anatomy, truly all influence the treatment. My goal is never to eliminate expression. It's to create balance while allowing the patient to continue looking like themselves. With hyaluronic acid injectables, we're thinking a bit differently. Now placement and depth becomes incredibly important. The face is really a three-dimensional structure and filler can really behave differently depending on where and how it's placed. I need to understand not only where I'm injecting, but the anatomical plane I'm working in and the structures around it. That understanding is important for both the aesthetic result and patient safety. Technique also means knowing how much product to use. More isn't necessarily better. Sometimes a very small amount placed thoughtfully can create a meaningful improvement. Sometimes the best decision is really not to inject a particular area at all. After more than three decades of working with facial anatomy, both surgically and aesthetically, one principle that has remained very consistent for me is that I have to respect the anatomy. The face isn't a blank canvas. It's a complex dynamic structure and every treatment has to work within that structure. So when injectable treatments are performed thoughtfully, the goal shouldn't be for someone to look at you and immediately know what you've had done. They should simply see you as balanced, refreshed, natural. So the product choice matters, but really understanding where to place it, how to place it, and how much to use. And when not to use it is really where the technique becomes an art.
why: Doctor explains his anatomy-first technique, which builds authority but lacks a scroll-stopping open.
opening_line: One of the most important things that I tell patients about injectables is the product is only one part of the result.
closing_line: And when not to use it is really where the technique becomes an art.
subject: why injector technique matters
claim: The same product gives different results in different hands; anatomy, placement, depth and restraint matter more than product.

transcript: This will probably upset some people, but I truly believe that skin cycling is just common sense packaged up into a marketing concept to make you buy into it. It is not the breakthrough the internet thinks it is, and it's something that I really need to address. But I'm not a needless hater, so I'm going to explain why I think this and what I would do instead. Let's take your basic skin cycling routine for example. I know there are loads of variations, but let's stick to the most common one. You start with a retinoid. Then on night two, use a chemical exfoliant. And on night three, you take a rest, and then you repeat the cycle. Again, not a needless hater, so there are pros to this, which I will acknowledge. First of all, it's easy to follow if you're a beginner. I think it also puts you in the right direction because you're using the right active ingredients to get where you want to be most of the time for acne. And I also like that it discourages layering the activives, but you can't layer the activives anyway. Even a beginner who's introducing these activives is probably going to go on Google and search, can I use this and this together? They're going to find out no. So, they're going to use them on different days anyway. Secondly, your skin has no concept of time. People will rave about one of the benefits of skin cycling being your skin not getting irritated because you're using activives on separate days. Your skin doesn't know you're using it on separate days. Your skin doesn't care if you use it on Tuesday and Thursday. It's not going to be like, well, I'm not going to overreact because you used it with a couple of days in between, which leads me to my third point, which is my biggest gripe about it. This technique leads people who haven't used either active to introduce them at the same time, which is a big fat no. And fourth, because you know there's a fourth skin cycling in the way it's been described is going to take you a long time to see the retinoid benefits that you see all over the internet. You're missing out on retinoid progress because you're spacing it out too much. You're trying to do six things at once. With all that being said, this is what I would do instead. I would just introduce your retinoid first. For most people, it's not easy to tolerate a retinoid. So, you definitely want to do one thing before the other thing. And the retinoid is hardest to adjust to. So, I recommend adjusting to it before you add in a chemical exfoliant approximately for 2 or 3 months. So, you can start to see the benefits and your skin can go through the retinization process that's missing out on if you're adding a chemical exfoliant in and hoping that it survives. And then, if you want to, you can add in a chemical exfoliant after say month 2, three or four. And this is what an example retinoid routine might look like. I don't need to see hate on trends for reviews. This is my honest opinion. I just knew people weren't going to like it.

In my daily work, I am seeing more and more often the traces that radical weight loss can leave on the face.

title: Dr. Ariel Ostad Treats the Glabellar Lines Using Jeuveau
transcript: Before I perform any injectable treatment, I always begin with an assessment. Even when we're treating an area as specific as the frown lines between the eyebrows, every patient has a slightly different anatomy, pattern, a movement, and a degree of muscle activity. Today, we're going to be treating the glabella lines with Juvo. Juvo is the botulinum toxin type A injectable, indicated for the temporary improvement in the appearance of moderate to severe glabella lines in adults. Before I treat you, I want to see exactly how your muscles are functioning. So can you please relax your face for me? First, I look at the face completely at rest. I'm looking at the lines that are already visible, the position of the brows, and whether there's any natural asymmetry from one side to the other. So now frown for me as strongly as you can. Good. When she frowns, we can see the activity of the muscles that are responsible for creating these lines, primarily what we call the corrugator muscles located on either side and the procerus muscle centrally. So relax again and frown one more time. What I'm assessing here isn't simply the line itself. I'm looking at the underlying muscle activity that's creating that line, where the muscles are positioned, how strongly they're contracting, and whether that movement is really symmetrical. It's important because I don't approach every patient exactly the same way. With Juvo, the goal is to temporarily reduce the muscle activity responsible for the moderate to severe glabella lines and therefore improve their appearance. For me, a thoughtful treatment begins with understanding the individual patient's anatomy rather than simply looking at a wrinkle and treating it. One more frown for me, perfect. Now that I've seen how your muscles behave both at rest and with movement, I can plan the treatment appropriately. The injection itself may only take a few minutes, but the assessment beforehand is really what allows us to approach the treatment with precision. Juvo temporarily improves the look of moderate to severe frown lines between the eyebrows and adults. There are risks of treatment. Effects of Juvo may spread hours to weeks after injection, causing serious symptoms. Alert your doctor right away of difficulty swallowing, speaking, breathing, eye problems, or muscle weakness, which can be signs of a life-threatening condition. If this happens, do not drive a car, operate machinery, or do other dangerous activities. For complete safety information, see at Juvo Way of a List PI or visit evillisrx.com. Ask your doctor if Juvo is right for you.

caption:
I nearly didn't post this. I filmed it yesterday morning, just before walking in to have two skin cancers removed.

I've decided to share it because I think there's a much bigger conversation to be had about health insurance. 

For those of us lucky enough to have it, we pay for it year after year believing it'll be there when we need it. But how many of us really understand exactly what we're covered for?

I'm lucky. I was able to get the treatment my specialist recommended. But what happens to someone who gets the same answer from their insurer and simply doesn't have the money to pay for it themselves?

I'm going to dig into this properly here, and we'll be talking a lot more about it on our podcast, Forking Good with Kate and Simon.

If you've ever thought you were covered by your insurance and then discovered you weren't, I'd really like to hear your story.

The surgery is done and I'm doing okay.

More to come.
Simon

caption:
Exosomes are extracellular vesicles, tiny nano-sized particles naturally secreted by cells, that act as biological messengers. They carry proteins, growth factors, and genetic material between cells, playing a critical role in cell-to-cell communication, tissue repair, and regeneration. In dermatology, harnessing the power of exosomes means we can now stimulate the skin’s own healing mechanisms at a cellular level, without the need for invasive procedures.

We are still in the early stages of our journey with exosome therapy in dermatology. While the science is promising, it is important to acknowledge that long-term data and large-scale clinical trials are still emerging. More research is needed before we can draw definitive conclusions, but evidence-based medicine has always required a starting point, and the early signals here are encouraging. I am committed to following the evidence as it evolves and to being transparent with my patients every step of the way.

If you would like to find out whether exosome therapy is right for you, comment ‘Treatment’ below and I will send you a link to book a consultation.

#Sculptra #MedicinaEstetica #Bioestimuladores #Colageno #DraDaniellaMorelos
transcript: Sabías que Sculptra no se convierte en colágeno? Lo interesante es saber cómo estimula tu cuerpo para producirlo. Sculptra está compuesto por ácido poliláctico, un material biocompatible y biodegradable que utilizamos como biostimulador. Cuando lo aplicamos, sus micropartículas generan una respuesta inflamatoria localizada que favorece la activación de fibroblastos. ¿Y por qué es tan importante esto? Porque los fibroblastos son las células encargadas de la producción de colágeno, principalmente de tipo 1 y tipo 3, que participan en la estructura y soporte a nuestra piel. A este proceso lo llamamos neocolagenesis. Y lo interesante es que no buscamos un efecto inmediato, sino una remodelación progresiva del tejido durante las siguientes semanas y meses. Por eso me gusta tanto la discriminación, no se trata simplemente de agregar volumen, sino de aprovechar la capacidad de respuesta de nuestro propio cuerpo.

title: Dr. Ariel Ostad Explains Cold-X Technology
transcript: When we talk about advances in injectable fillers, we tend to focus on what happens when the product is injected. But something that's equally important that happens long before the filler ever reaches the patient, it really happens during the manufacturing process. Evelise is a collection of hyaluronic acid injectables made using something called cold-ex technology. That temperature actually plays in preserving the hyaluronic acid molecule. Hyaluronic acid, otherwise known as HA, is a molecule that occurs naturally within our skin and all our tissues, connective tissue. And one of its important properties is its ability to bind water. But hyaluronic acid is also sensitive to the way it's processed. This is where the key important thing is. Traditional filler manufacturing can involve heat during the cross-linking process and heat can contribute to the breakdown or sort of what we call fragmentation of that hyaluronic acid chains. Cold-ex technology takes really a different approach. It uses near freezing temperature during the manufacturing process. The goal is a filler that's designed to perform better within the treatment area while looking and feeling natural. And within the Evelise collection, we can currently have Evelise form, which has a little more structure. Evelise smooth, which is therefore smoother, and both are made using cold-ex technology. And they have really different, what we call viscoelastic properties, different viscosities. And this way allows us to select a product that's based on the treatment goal. And for me, as a physician and an artist, this is where science really becomes clinically relevant. We're not simply looking at how much volume a filler can create. We're thinking more about the properties of the gel, how it behaves within a dynamic area of the face, and ultimately how that translates into the result we see and feel. Patients today are increasingly telling me the same thing. They want natural results. They don't want to look like they've had filler. They want to remain and maintain their expression. caption:
#EnsembleContreLaDésinformation pour qu’ensemble, on mette fin aux mythes dangereux, comme celui que « la crème solaire cause le cancer »! ❌

Eh non! Ce n’est pas la crème solaire qui cause le cancer de la peau, mais bien le soleil! 🌞

La recherche scientifique nous a permis de comprendre que les rayons ultraviolets du soleil sont des agents mutagènes qui endommagent l’ADN, et que l’accumulation de mutations non réparées est la principale cause des carcinomes et des mélanomes (cancers de la peau). 

Le paradoxe de la crème solaire, un concept avancé par le Dr Ivan Litvinov, nous indique que la crème solaire procure un faux sentiment de protection à ses utilisateurs, qui se retrouvent alors plus exposés aux rayons UV. C’est ce qui expliquerait la hausse des cas de cancer de la peau chez les utilisateurs de crème solaire, et non pas la crème solaire elle-même.

Néanmoins, la crème solaire, combinée à d’autres mesures de protection (vêtements anti-UV, chercher l’ombre, éviter le soleil à son pic, etc.) demeure la meilleure stratégie pour profiter du beau temps tout en protégeant sa santé. 

Merci à @scienceupfirst pour cette initiative pour lutter contre la désinformation.

title: Dr. Ariel Ostad: The Less Is More Approach
transcript: After more than 30 years of treating patients, one of the things I've come to believe very strongly about is that in aesthetics, less is often more. When a patient comes into my office, my goal isn't to change the way they look. It's to understand what makes their face uniquely theirs and to preserve it. Every face has its own proportions, expressions, asymmetries, and characteristics. Those aren't necessarily things we need to correct. They are part of what makes someone recognizable. So when I assess a patient, I don't start by asking, what can I inject? I ask, what does this patient actually need? And sometimes the answer is very little. Sometimes it's nothing at all. I think we have reached an interesting point in aesthetic medicine where we have more tools available to us than ever before. But just because we can do something doesn't necessarily mean we should. For me, a successful treatment shouldn't announce itself. I don't want someone to walk into a room and have people think she had filler or he had something done. I want people to think, you look great. Maybe they can't even identify why. To me, that's the difference between changing someone's face and refining it. I'm not trying to eliminate every single line. I'm not trying to remove every sign of aging. And I'm certainly not trying to make every patient look the same. Aging to me is part of being human. And my roles to understand where a thoughtful intervention can make a meaningful difference without really taking away the character of the face. That's also why I tend to take really a gradual approach. We can always reassess. We can always enhance later further. We can always do more when it's appropriate. But restraint really gives us the ability to preserve balance, expression and proportion along the way. And after really decades of working with the face, I have developed a tremendous respect for its complexity and really perhaps an even greater respect for knowing when to leave something alone. My philosophy is really simple. Don't chase perfection. Preserve the individual. Use the right treatment in the right place for the right patient and only as much as you truly need. Because ultimately, the best aesthetic work shouldn't make you look like someone else. It should allow you to look like the best version of yourself.

We're starting to see effects of sun, we're starting to see effects of loss of collagen and elastin so procedures should be directed towards those things. So energy based treatments like IPL, laser resurfacing as well as chemical peels can be helpful and in my office I have an amazing team of estheticians, dermatologists and plastic surgeons that can help you with invasive and non-invasive ways of approaching that. Now what are some surgical procedures that patients in their 30s are looking for? Well for men it's still gynecomastia is a number one requested procedure, sometimes liposuction they have diminutive lengths. caption:
This is what people do not understand about facial filler.

It does not always stay as a perfect little “lift” exactly where it was placed.

With special imaging, filler can show up almost like a map inside the face — and when highlighted in green, you can actually see where it has spread, layered, and sometimes migrated over time.

That matters.

Because filler is hydrophilic.

It can draw water.

Not once.

Not twice.

But repeatedly over time.

So a face that was supposed to look lifted and refreshed can slowly start to look heavier, puffier, wider, or less defined.

This is why I am so careful about simply “adding more.”

More filler is not always more youthful.

Sometimes it is just more weight, more water attraction, and more distortion.

The goal is not to fill every hollow.

The goal is to understand the face before you start changing it.
